https://www.egyptindependent.com/witkoff.text: Kyiv, Ukraine — US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner pushed for a return to trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine on Sunday after “substantive” discussions with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv. It marks their first visit to the Ukrainian capital since the war began and comes amid near-constant Russian missile and drone strikes on the city. Although no major breakthroughs were announced after Sunday’s talks, Witkoff said he was “confident that there’ll be a good resolution here.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said “several new ideas” were discussed during “good discussions” with the US, but did not expand on what those ideas were. The talks followed intensive meetings Witkoff and Kushner held with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, part of Washington’s renewed push to end the war in Ukraine. “One thing Steve (Witkoff) and I really thought would be productive is to go back to the trilateral format, which we were able to do about six months ago,” Kushner said in a news conference following the talks in Kyiv Kushner said he prefers trilateral talks as they allow all parties to communicate directly, without the US having to speak for Ukraine or Russia. “Everyone was speaking, you know, in Russian to each other and really discussing these issues in a very actually friendly manner, all in Russian,” he said of previous rounds of trilateral negotiations. He added that the US had spoken with both parties about this idea, adding that “hopefully we’ll have progress on that very soon.” Previous trilateral talks mediated by the US have failed to resolve key issues such as territory and security guarantees for Ukraine. Zelensky agreed, saying that “we must do everything possible to ensure that trilateral meetings take place – or trilateral meetings plus our European partners. We’ll see what Russia agrees to.” Speaking about his recent visit to Russia, Witkoff said his team had a “good, concrete conversation” with Putin. “If you don’t have relationships with both sides, and you have poor communication, then you probably have very, very little chance of getting to a peaceful resolution,” Witkoff said. Three rounds of talks The US-Ukraine talks concluded on Sunday evening local time after two rounds of discussion, followed by a third round of negotiations with European representatives. Officials from the United Kingdom, France and Germany were present in Kyiv, according to Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the Ukrainian Presidency. Zelensky said Ukraine, Europe and the US planned to meet again “in the near future.” “We want to prevent loss of life, we want this war to end fairly for all of us, and we want it to end in such a way that Russia’s aggression against Ukraine is never repeated,” Zelensky said during an earlier press briefing following the first round of talks. “I believe that every meeting like this will bring us closer to that goal,” he added. T-shirts with the slogan “Kyiv regime” were prepared by the Ukrainian president as gifts for attendees of the talks, according to Serhiy Nykyforov, Zelensky’s press secretary. Upon their arrival in the Ukrainian capital, the US envoys were taken on a tour of a cathedral in central Kyiv damaged in Russian attacks. St. Sophia’s Cathedral, which is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, sustained damage to its windows and window frames. On Friday, CNN reported on a Russian strike hitting Ukraine’s Security Service headquarters in Kyiv, which also affected the cathedral. Ahead of their meeting, the Ukrainian president thanked Trump for allowing the trip to happen “from a security standpoint,” adding that Ukraine had been “waiting a long time” for Witkoff and Kushner’s visit. Zelensky stressed on Sunday that an acute shortage of air defense interceptors has left Ukraine vulnerable to ballistic missile attacks, calling it the country’s “weak spot.” “The US side will increase production volumes of Patriot anti-ballistic missiles next year,” Zelensky said. “We’re counting on such systems to defend our country, so we’ll increase the volume next year – I’m confident of that.” Journey to Kyiv Witkoff and Kushner made a stop in the Polish city of Rzeszow en route from Moscow to Kyiv, Russian state media outlet TASS reported. The plane landed at 1:31 a.m. local time. The US envoys continued their journey to Kyiv by rail, with Witkoff later saying, “I didn’t like the train. I loved the train.” Russia and Ukraine have enacted a 72-hour temporary truce for the duration of the US envoys’ visits, specifically halting airstrikes on each other’s capitals, Kyiv and Moscow. The halt in strikes began at midnight on Friday into Saturday and will last for the duration of the weekend of diplomacy. The truce applies only to the two capitals. In overnight attacks into Sunday, Russia continued its bombardment of Ukraine while avoiding the city of Kyiv. According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russian forces launched 108 Shahed-type drones from Russia, while at least three people were killed in the latest strikes and infrastructure was hit in the Kyiv region. Russian airstrikes were recorded in 11 locations across Ukraine, while a large-scale fire has been extinguished at an infrastructure facility in Kyiv region as a result of a Russian strike. In total, 10 Ukrainian civilians have been killed over the past 24 hours, and a further 65 have been injured. Witkoff and Kushner began their whirlwind weekend of diplomacy with a three-hour meeting with Putin at the Kremlin on Saturday afternoon. The negotiations were followed by dinner with the Russian leader, according to a Kremlin press briefing. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff greets Russian President Vladimir Putin during a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow, Russia on Saturday. Mikhail Metzel/Sputnik/Pool/Reuters Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov later described the talks as “useful” and said the American representatives had “prepared seriously for this trip.” He said the US team expressed interest in ending hostilities as quickly as possible and offered “a whole series of considerations regarding possible paths to a settlement.” A White House official said both sides “discussed substantive plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks.” CNN’s Tim Lister, Charlotte Reck, Jonny Hallam and Victoria Butenko contributed to this report.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Wooroora station in far north Queensland which could soon be bought by Bush Heritage. Photograph: Supplied View image in fullscreen Wooroora station in far north Queensland which could soon be bought by Bush Heritage. Photograph: Supplied Queensland ‘Worldwide legacy’: almost $20m raised to protect majestic tract of land in far north Queensland Bush Heritage hopes to buy Wooroora station, which links wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland and is home to 12 endangered species Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Joe Hinchliffe Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.06 EDT Last modified on Wed 28 Oct 2026 17.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A majestic tract of land in far north Queensland that links wet tropics and world heritage rainforest, and contains headwaters that flow to the Great Barrier Reef, could be bought and protected by Christmas, after a conservation group raised more than $19m in private donations to buy the cattle station. map Wooroora spans more than 20,000 hectares of largely intact wet sclerophyll forest and savanna woodland on the lands of the Jirrbal people about 100km south-west of Cairns – and borders Bush Heritage’s existing 43,575-hectare Yourka Reserve in one of the most biodiverse regions in Australia . Cassowary and tree-kangaroos are among at least 12 threatened species and more than 30 species of conservation significance that have already been recorded on Wooroora, which is also the northernmost refuge for koalas, and, according to the would-be owners, is almost certainly home to species yet unknown to science. View image in fullscreen Wooroora station is the most northerly habitat for koalas. Photograph: John Wybrow In 2024 a plan to clear more than 500ha of Wooroora station for a 42-turbine windfarm was rejected because of what the then environment minister, Tanya Plibersek, described as the unacceptable impact on the environment, including the spectacled flying-fox and the northern greater glider. The chief executive of Bush Heritage, Rachel Lowry, said Wooroora would be the organisation’s most ambitious single acquisition in its 35-year history to date. “This breaks the glass ceiling,” Lowry said. “And I don’t think it’s just for Bush Heritage, but for our sector more broadly.” Lowry said fundraising for the $24.7m to buy and manage the land for an initial five years has been going on for more than 18 months. She travelled to New York during the 2025 UN climate summit to make a presentation that helped result in a donation of almost $2.5m from the foundation associated with the US outdoor clothing company Patagonia. View image in fullscreen Rachel Lowry at Wooroora station Given the country is a global biodiversity hotspot, Lowry said the protection “forever” of Wooroora was “not just a gift for Australia”. “When we step in and we protect and manage country, like Wooroora, we’re leaving a legacy worldwide,” she said. An anonymous Australian philanthropist also donated $6m. Now Bush Heritage is appealing to the public to raise the final $5.3m it needs by the deadline of 24 December. Jirrbal senior elder Uncle Kurt Noble said the land purchase would allow traditional owners back on “proper Jirrbal land”. “There are a lot of stories within the family connected to this country,” he said. “Some of the Dreamtime stories, as well as a little bit of the history”. In a recorded interview from Wooroora provided by Bush Heritage, Noble said his great-grandmother was born on the station but that he had not previously had the opportunity to visit. View image in fullscreen A Lumholtz tree-kangaroo mother and baby at Wooroora station. Photograph: BG Thomson “Much of our land is under private ownership, you know, and to have access, to be able to come back and forward, has been very restricted over many years – over generations,” he said. Renewed access would not only enable care and restoration for the environment, he said, but also for “the cultural values of our land”. Noble said it would allow “our young people to grow up with a better understanding, not only of country, but of language, of song, of our cultural practices, of our different significant sites all over this country”. Traditional custodian and the Wabubadda Aboriginal Corporation chair, Liam Roberts, said in another recorded video that Jirrbal were hoping to jointly manage the reserve. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “We’ve got rangers. We’ve got work we’d like to do on country,” he said. Roberts said the station contained “sacred artefacts” along old Jirrbal trails and creeks. “It’s beautiful camping country, it’s beautiful fishing country, it’s beautiful ecology,” he said. “In the old days the pathways were very much running from the dry country to the wet country, seasonally, and this is a key part of country that we can’t find anywhere else.” Bush Heritage’s head of Queensland and the Northern Territory, Dr Jo Axford, said Wooroora includes one of the region’s largest unprotected stretches of wet sclerophyll forest – towering eucalyptus grandis that forms a transition zone between ancient wet tropics rainforest and seasonally dry savannah woodlands. From its neighbouring reserve at Yourka, Bush Heritage had been actively seeking to acquire the station since 2010 because it provides the “missing piece” in a 429,000-hectare nature corridor that runs up to Cape York. View image in fullscreen Uncle Kurt Noble, senior Jirrbal elder, said securing access to the land was vital for future generations. Photograph: Supplied “The amazing thing about Wooroora is that it’s this long, narrow property – if you look at a map, Wooroora itself is almost like a key,” Axford said. Wooroora rises to about 1,000m above sea level, but falls to 660m in 10km, which Axford said creates a diverse mosaic of habitat that will allow threatened species such as the critically endangered magnificent brood frog to find refuges and hopefully adapt to a changing climate. This “really unusual” topography makes Wooroora one of the only places on Earth home to both the rainforest dwelling southern cassowary and the plains roaming emu, where Lumholtz’s tree-kangaroo clamber through canopies near koalas, she said. But Axford said she is confident the station also harboured undescribed species. “Nobody’s looked at the invertebrates, nobody has gone into all those gullies and valleys, these huge rhyolite outcrops,” she said. “I’ve had the advantage of being able to fly over it in a chopper – and you just know there must be so many hidden secrets in there”.
